title: Building the State
subtitle: Ten years to make the machinery a country runs on.
objectives: Describe how the Commonwealth prepared institutions
Explain the choice of a national language
Assess how ready the country was in 1941

cards.title: Ten years to build a state from the parts you have
cards.text: A flag and a date are the easy bits. The Commonwealth had to build the things a country runs on.

cards.title: The National Defense Act of 1935
cards.text: The first major law of the Commonwealth created an army from almost nothing.
points: **Douglas MacArthur** was brought in as military adviser.
**A reserve force** was to be trained over ten years.
**Funding was always short.**
**By 1941 it was far from ready.**

cards.title: One country, many languages
cards.text: A national language was chosen deliberately, and the choice was argued over.
points: **The 1935 Constitution** called for a national language.
**Tagalog was selected** as its basis in 1937.
**Not because it had the most speakers**: Cebuano had a strong claim.
**It was the language of Manila**, the centre of government and print.

cards.title: What it could and could not do
cards.text: Six powers. Three were held and three were kept in Washington.

question.text: Tagalog was chosen as the basis of the national language mainly because…
options: it was the language of Manila and of print
question.explain: Cebuano had a comparable number of speakers. Manila's position decided it.

cards.title: Naming a language is never only about language
cards.text: Choosing one region's tongue as everyone's is a political act, and people knew it.
points: **Speakers of other languages objected**, and still do.
**The name changed over time**: Pilipino, then Filipino.
**Filipino today** draws on more than Tagalog alone.
**The argument is not settled**, which is itself worth knowing.

cards.title: The two hardest problems
cards.text: One expanded. The other barely moved.
points: **Schools grew quickly**, in English and in the vernacular.
**Land reform was tried** and mostly failed.
**Tenant farmers stayed tenants.**
**That unfinished problem** returns again and again.

cards.title: Nation-building games make you pick, and so did they
cards.text: Limited budget, several things that all need funding, and a clock running. That was the Commonwealth.
points: **Spend on schools** and the army stays thin.
**Spend on the army** and land reform waits.
**They chose education**, and it showed in 1941.
**Every real government** is making this trade.

question.text: Land reform was largely achieved during the Commonwealth.
question.explain: It was tried and made very little progress. Tenancy remained the norm.

cards.title: Preparation is not the same as readiness
cards.text: Training for ten years and being ready are different claims, and 1941 tested the difference.
points: **A plan on paper** is not a trained army.
**Equipment was old** and there was not enough of it.
**The reserve was partly trained** when the invasion came.
**Preparation ran out of time.**

question.text: How ready was the Philippine military when Japan invaded?
question.explain: The reserve existed on paper more than in practice, and equipment was short.

cards.title: Self-rule meant writing your own laws
cards.alt: An old manual typewriter with a blank sheet rolled in, on a worn wooden desk with a brass lamp
cards.text: Land reform, education, labour. All passed here, by an assembly elected here.

terms.def: The 1935 law creating a Philippine army and reserve.
American general who advised on building that army.

cards.title: What to remember
points: The National Defense Act of 1935 built an army from almost nothing.
Tagalog was chosen in 1937, because of Manila rather than numbers.
Education expanded; land reform did not.
By 1941 preparation had run out of time.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 2 Social Studies, the second of the scope's two weeks on preparing for independence, taking the institutional view rather than repeating the political narrative. Three strands are followed (defence, language and land) because each has a different ending and together they show what preparation actually achieved. The language card is handled honestly: Tagalog was not chosen on numbers, the objection was real, and the argument is live, which is more useful to him than a settled-sounding fact. Land reform is flagged as the unfinished problem that returns under every administration later in the term.
discussion: Why was Tagalog chosen when Cebuano had similar numbers?
What is the difference between preparing and being ready?
Why does land reform keep coming back?
extension: Find out which languages are spoken in your own family's provinces.
List what an army needs besides soldiers.
misconceptions: That Tagalog was chosen because most people spoke it.
That a ten-year plan means ten years of readiness.
